# Riverine Heatwaves {#rh}

*Author: Tom Baumann*

*Supervisor: Henri Funk*

*Degree: Bachelor*

## Abstract

Riverine Heatwaves, which are prolonged periods of exceptionally high water temperatures in river systems, are a 
underexplored hydrological phenomenon, that is expected to gain considerable importance throughout the next years, also 
due to their link to climate change. The following paper will give an introduction to the precise definition of riverine 
heatwaves, as well as explain its drivers and impacts. Furthermore, it will focus on the methodology used to detect 
riverine heatwavesfrom temperature time series, and how their development, both spatially and temporally, can be 
quantified and assessed. This will be helpful, to gain a better understanding of riverine heatwaves. It will be 
especially important to explore how riverine heatwaves evolve during climate change, as all three metrics to quantify
frequency, duration and intensity seem to be increasing.

# Introduction

## Riverine Heatwaves Definition

Riverine Heatwaves are defined similarly to atmospheric heatwaves, as periods where daily mean water temperature 
exceeds a local seasonally varying percentile based threshold for a prolonged period of time. Usually, a historical 
baseline period is used, to calculate the threshold, which is then applied to the examined time series, of the same 
location. (hamel, hobday, chen)
Although the definition is similar, aquatic heatwaves and atmospheric heatwaves behave differently, as aquatic heatwaves 
tend to be more rare, but more persistent, than atmospheric heatwaves. (hamel)

## Drivers of Riverine Heatwaves

As riverine heatwaves are a phenomenon that has not gained much attention so far, its drivers are not fully understood 
yet. We know that river temperature in general is controlled by a variety of factors. There are the atmospheric 
conditions like air temperature, wind, rainfall and solar radiation, the hydrologic conditions which means the 
discharge and how the river interacts with different water bodies within its proximity and processes at the water 
stream bed interface, for example the interaction of the river with ground water. On top of that, the water temperature 
can be influenced by its environment, for example by the amount of vegetation and shading, by impervious surfaces nearby 
or by the presence of thermal effluents from near industries or human waste water.
However, so far very little is know on how riverine heatwaves are caused. It is assumed, that what leads to heatwaves 
are usually processes that include a number of these drivers.
From literature we know, that usually riverine heatwaves relate to high air temperature and solar radiation, low 
discharge and changes in water sources. Also they tend to appear most frequently above dams and in free-flowing rivers 
(hamel).
Although there have been some studies indicating correlations between these processes and riverine heatwaves, they are 
not fully understood yet, and there still remains a large knowledge gap.

 In general, river water temperature is controlled by atmospheric conditions (the energy budget at the air–water interface), hydrologic conditions (discharge and the interaction with different water bodies, such as lakes and tributaries), processes at the water–streambed interface (for example, groundwater–surface water interactions), the surrounding environment (for example, riparian vegetation, impervious surfaces and shading) and management impacts (for example, thermal effluents from industries and urban wastewater)14,59,60,61.  (hamel)
 
 Specifically, little is known about how different processes interact during the development of riverine heatwaves. These processes include high atmospheric energy inputs (dominated by intense solar radiation), slower streamflow velocities and reduced volume (permitting more time for heat absorption and lower thermal capacity, respectively), and changes in water sources (for example, reduced groundwater inflow, which normally cools rivers during the summer). ## Impacts of Riverine Heatwaves

The appearance of riverine heatwaves can have both ecological and socioeconomic impacts. These can be parted into 
different layers. Firstly there are the immediate effects of prolonged periods of high water temperature. The higher 
temperature could lead to an increased rate of open water evaporation. Moreover, they might lead to an increased spread 
of diseases, harmful algee bloom and a decrease in water quality in gerneral. This in turn can reduce the availability 
of drinking water or the possibility of recreational activities and be harmful to flora and fauna living in, or close by 
the river systems. Also the prolonged high temperatures can cause thermal stress on fish and other aquatic species. 
Together this is threatening fishing and aquaculture which is a vital source of food for a large part of the population (Chen).
Moreover, high water temperatures can also negatively impact energy production, as nuclear power production often 
relies on cooling water from close by river system, which already has been unavailable due to riverine heatwaves in some 
cases.

## Importance / research possibilities

Multiple studies have shown that mean river temperatures have increased over recent decades in different parts of the world, including in Europe21,25,30,62,63,64, North America22,65,66, the Eurasian Arctic67,68 and globally69.

Such an increase has already been documented in the United States, where the number of riverine heatwaves has doubled, with on average 11 heatwave days per year in 1996 to 25 in 20211. This rising trend in riverine heatwave occurrence appears to be outpacing that of atmospheric heatwaves24.

Although changes in mean water temperature have received considerable scientific attention, it remains to be investigated how they translate to changes in riverine heatwaves.

- Riverine heatwaves are rather unexplored

- Challenges: 
  - Universally used definition,
  - Wide network of long term daily river temperature data

- Make projections: 
  - Understand its drivers (and how they interact to cause heatwaves)

models: Finally, the construction of reliable models to forecast and predict future riverine heatwave occurrence requires calibration and evaluation data to ensure robust performance and quantify and constrain their uncertainty. Models developed on limited data often fail when applied beyond their original scope or for the projection of extremes83,84,85. Using datasets that cover diverse elevation and climate zones is probably going to improve model accuracy, because it enables capturing a broader range of water temperature regimes, which is especially important when studying riverine heatwaves.
Water temperature models are essential tools for quantifying the contributions of different driving processes of water temperature (for example, refs. 18,25) and to generate water temperature forecasts and future projections (for example, refs. 34,73). However, they might not yet be fit for the purpose of modelling riverine heatwaves.

All of these models share some limitations. First, all model types are mostly evaluated in terms of their overall accuracy, and are less often evaluated on their performance during extremely high temperatures79,102,103,104, and hardly ever specifically on riverine heatwaves31. Second, most existing models do not incorporate information on streamflow partitioning, such as meltwater and groundwater contributions, which have been shown to influence the development of extreme water temperatures25. Consequently, the ability of currently available set-ups to model riverine heatwaves is limited and not yet fully understood.

Based on the above, we are calling for the development of a centralized database of open-source river water temperature data75.

# Methods

## Data

For the analysis we will use a data set of longitudinal temperature data from 14 gauges at Main river system in Bavaria. 
The data set includes eight measurements of water temperature per day over a time period of 5 to 20 years between 2000 
and 2020.
Literature suggests, that the analysis of riverine heatwaves requires time series of at least 10, ideally 30 years with 
at least daily data and not more than 50 percent, ideally not more than 25 percent of missing data. 
Also for this analysis it will be necessary to have a common time period for all stations, to obtain comparable results 
between stations. As many of the stations do not cover a common time period, and as some of the stations have a 
high amount of missing data for some years, the analysis has be limited to six of the stations to guarantee these 
standards. Excluding the other stations gives us a 15 year common period time series of daily water temperature, with 
almost no missing values (not more than ten percent per yearly station specific time series).
The used stations are marked in figure 1, which also shows their position along the main river system.

## Threshold

The threshold which classifies riverine heatwaves has to be precisely defined. This paper is going to use the definition
of Hobday, adopted originally from marine heatwaves. However this definition has also been widely used in work on 
riverine heatwaves (hamel, chen, ,...).

The definition of marine heatwaves by Hobday uses a 90th percentile seasonally varying threshold, which is also varying 
with location and therefore calculated separately for each station. To calculate the seasonally varying threshold, for 
each day the historical temperature measurements, as well as the historical measurements from a 11 day surrounding 
window are taken. From these data points, the 90 percent quantile is taken. The exact formula for this calculation is 
depicted below, where i is... and x is...(Hobday 2016) This procedure will be repeated for each day of year, until the 
threshold for the entire year is completed. 
Usually, for this a historical baseline period is used. But since here the data set only covers a relatively short time 
period, the same time period is used for the calculation of the threshold and the analysis. Even if the same threshold 
definition is used, comparing results from different studies on riverine heatwaves has to be treated carefully. It can 
be problematic to compare exact numbers for metrics between studies with different baseline periods, as climate change 
suggests a temperature biased over time. However, as in this paper the focus is only to demonstrate how heatwaves evolve 
relatively to another over time by looking for general trends rather than comparing exact metrics with other studies, 
and in this paper only measurements from the same stations with the same baseline period are going to compared, this 
approach also suffices.

Resulting from this procedure, we obtain a threshold for each station, that can be used for comparison with the time 
series of each year. In figure 2 an example of this is shown for the Kemmern station and the year 2018. Heatwaves can 
then be detected, by firstly marking all potential candidates, all days exceeding the thresholds. After, the time series 
are examined for events of at least five consecutive days exceeding the threshold. These are marked as heatwaves and 
given an ID, while all short events are discarded. When there is a gap of only one or two days between two or more
heatwaves that all individually have a duration of at least five days, the heatwaves, are merged into one heatwave.

## Metrics used

This paper will focus on three primary metrics, that will be used to quantify the evolution of riverine heatwaves. We 
will use a frequency metric, a duration metric and an intensity metric, to be able to describe the evolution under 
different aspects.

To quantify the evolution of frequency, for each heatwave the number of heatwave events per year will be used. This 
will be Calculated per station, or may be summarized over different stations or years. For the calculation, we will use 
the IDs given to the heatwaves.
1. Frequency

  Heatwave events: number of heatwaves per year
  formula

summary statistics for each heatwave
Furthermore, we will consider the duration of the heatwaves. This is calculated using the first and last day of each 
heatwave (see formula 1). The duration plays an important role, as especially longer heatwaves can have more severs 
impacts.
2. Duration

  Duration: duration of a heatwaves
  formula
  
Lastly, we will use intensity, to assess the amount of the heat spike. The intensity, is defined as the temperature, by 
which the heatwave threshold is exceeded. In this paper it is defined, as the mean of this temperature exceedence per 
heatwave. (see formula)
3. Intensity

For results of studies to be consistent, it is important to have a clear common definition of metrics. 
  Intensity: mean exceedance of threshold per heatwave
  formula

These metrics can also be used to summarize two or more of these characteristics. For example, the heatwave events can 
be multiplied with the mean annual duration, to obtain the number of heatwave days per year. Or the duration of a 
heatwave can be multiplied with its mean intensity, to obtain its mean severity. 

## Research Question

This paper examines the evolution of riverine heatwaves over climate change. Therefore we want to focus primarily on 
the changes over time, using the period of the used data. To do this, we will examine the development of the three 
previously defined metrics and pose the following questions:

1. How has the frequency of riverine heatwaves changed over time?

2. How has the duration of riverine heatwaves changed over time?

3. How has the intensity of riverine heatwaves changed over time?

Given the availability of stations with different locations along the same river system, we will also look into, how 
the metrics differ between the stations.

# Research

Dense monitoring networks along individual rivers could facilitate a better understanding of the small-scale variability of processes leading to riverine heatwaves and on how processes generating riverine heatwaves change from upstream to downstream or from low-order to high-order streams82.
